routes.description: Justify Hirsi Ali's Christian turn by connecting transformative personal experience and chosen faith with Christianity's moral character, inherited institutions, and claimed necessity for Western civilizational renewal.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that her experience provides a legitimate personal basis for conversion, that Christianity offers a defensible affirmative moral framework, and that renewing it answers a consequential institutional and ideological vacuum not adequately filled by secular alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect personal transformation, Christian truth commitments, and civilizational need into a sufficient justification for Hirsi Ali's Christian turn.

centralBridges.description: Explain how the crisis, prayer, perceived encounter with a higher reality, and recovery can rationally support a personal commitment to Christianity.
Establish that Christianity's central teachings and exemplar provide an affirmative moral vision materially distinct from the rival religious ideology under discussion.
Show that the removal of Christian formation created an institutional moral vacuum and that Christian renewal can supply what secular alternatives have not organized or transmitted.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why inherited faith, education, organization, and active counter-messaging are needed to transmit the proposed moral framework across generations.
Require criticism of Christian institutions to identify a viable replacement capable of moral formation and resistance to destructive ideological recruitment.

routes.description: Reject the proposed justification by separating psychological or social benefits from the truth of Christianity's supernatural claims, challenging its asserted moral authority, and identifying rational secular resources for morality and ideological resistance.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that personal recovery and civilizational usefulness do not demonstrate Christian truth, that Christianity's doctrines or institutions cannot simply be assumed morally authoritative, and that rational secular alternatives defeat the claim of religious necessity.

motionBridge.description: Require the Christian turn to satisfy a truth test independent of consolation, meaning, institutional utility, or desirable social consequences.

centralBridges.description: Identify Christianity's definite supernatural commitments and require evidence proportionate to their universe-defining factual significance.
Test whether Christian doctrines and institutions merit the moral authority assigned to them rather than deriving that authority from their religious status.
Show that humanism, rational inquiry, and moral philosophy can supply standards of judgment without adding supernatural beliefs.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the consoling, motivational, or organizational effects of faith from evidence that its existential propositions are true.
Explain how enlightened rationality can oppose dangerous ideology without using a less extreme religious commitment as a protective instrument.

sections.title: Personal experience and conversion
sections.rationale: The motion expressly places Hirsi Ali's crisis, prayer, recovery, and chosen commitment against the objection that a transformative experience alone cannot establish a particular religion.

sections.title: Supernatural truth and practical benefit
sections.rationale: The central truth-test clash asks whether meaning, consolation, and social usefulness can justify belief when Christianity also makes definite factual claims about supernatural reality.

sections.title: Christian moral character and religious distinction
sections.rationale: The civilizational case depends on Christianity's moral content and its claimed distinction from Islam, while the opposing route contests both its doctrines and the asserted categorical difference.

sections.title: Moral formation and secular alternatives
sections.rationale: The alleged moral vacuum must be tested against secular humanism and moral philosophy, including whether either religious or secular institutions can transmit an effective framework to younger generations.

sections.title: Civilizational defense and ideological resistance
sections.rationale: The concluding burden concerns whether renewed Christian belief is needed to resist Islamist recruitment and defend Western inheritance or whether rationality can answer the threat without religion.
